  filter(event_name == "SQL Symphony Concert") %>%
  mutate(date_formatted = ymd(as.character(date))) %>%  # Convert numeric to date

  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "Variable", 
               values_to = "Missing_Count") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Variable, 
              values_from = Missing_Count)

R-2: I can write well documented and tidy code.

Example of ggplot2 plotting

{r}
#| label: r-2-1

# Lab 4 Question 7 - Well-formatted ggplot with clear structure
data_plot <- ca_childcare |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool),
    names_to = "age_group",
    values_to = "price"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    age_group = str_remove(age_group, "mc_"),
    age_group = str_to_title(age_group),
    age_group = fct_relevel(age_group, "Infant", "Toddler", "Preschool")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = study_year, y = price, color = census_region)) + 
  geom_point(size = 0.8) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) + 
  facet_wrap(~ age_group) +
  labs(
    x = "Study Year",
    y = "Weekly Median Price for Center-Based Childcare ($)",
    color = "California Region"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2008, 2018, 2)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )

data_plot

Example of function formatting

{r}
#| label: r-2-3

# Lab 8 Question 3 - Well-documented plotting function
plot_boxplot <- function(data, x_var, y_var) {
  
  # Get variable names as strings for labels
  x_label <- rlang::as_label(rlang::enquo(x_var))
  y_label <- rlang::as_label(rlang::enquo(y_var))
  
  # Create readable labels
  x_title <- str_to_title(str_replace_all(x_label, "_", " "))
  y_title <- str_to_title(str_replace_all(y_label, "_", " "))
  
  # Create the plot
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{ x_var }}, y = {{ y_var }}, fill = {{ x_var }})) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(
      x = x_title,
      y = y_title,
      title = paste(y_title, "by", x_title)
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    guides(fill = "none")  # Remove legend due to double encoding
}

Example (function stops)

{r}
#| label: r-3-function-stops

# Challenge 7 Question 2 - Function with comprehensive input validation
replace_outliers <- function(measurements, min_value, max_value) {
  
  # Check that measurements is numeric
  if (!is.numeric(measurements)) {
    stop("measurements must be numeric")
  }
  
  # Check that min and max values are numeric
  if (!is.numeric(min_value) | !is.numeric(max_value)) {
    stop("min_value and max_value must be numeric")
  }
  
  # Check that min and max are single values
  if (length(min_value) != 1 | length(max_value) != 1) {
    stop("min_value and max_value must be single values")
  }
  
  # Check that min is less than max
  if (min_value >= max_value) {
    stop("min_value must be less than max_value")
  }
  
  # Replace outliers with NA
  case_when(
    measurements < min_value ~ NA_real_,
    measurements > max_value ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ measurements
  )
}

Dates (time series plot)

{r}
#| label: dvs-1-date

# Challenge 7 Question 5 - Time series showing change over years
fish_summary <- fish |>
  drop_na(condition_index) |>
  group_by(year, species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_condition = mean(condition_index, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 5) |>
  mutate(species = fct_reorder2(species, year, mean_condition))

ggplot(fish_summary, aes(x = year, y = mean_condition, color = species)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Fish Condition Index Over Time by Species",
    subtitle = "Yearly averages for groups with n ≥ 5 observations",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean Condition Index",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

PE-2: I can write functions to reduce repetition in my code.

Example 1: Function that operates on vectors

{r}
#| label: pe-2-1

# Lab 7 Question 4 - Rescaling function for vectors
rescale_01 <- function(x) {
  if (!is.numeric(x)) {
    stop("Input must be numeric")
  }
  
  if (length(x) <= 1) {
    stop("Input must have more than one element")
  }
  
  min_x <- min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  max_x <- max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  (x - min_x) / (max_x - min_x)
}

Example 2: Function that operates on data frames

{r}
#| label: pe-2-2

# Lab 8 Question 1 - Function that operates on data frames
rescale_column <- function(data, cols) {
  data |> 
    mutate(
      across(.cols = {{ cols }}, 
             .fns = rescale_01)
    )
}

Example 3: Function that operates on vectors or data frames

{r}
#| label: pe-2-3

# Challenge 7 Question 2 - Function with multiple vector inputs
replace_outliers <- function(measurements, min_value, max_value) {
  
  if (!is.numeric(measurements)) {
    stop("measurements must be numeric")
  }
  
  if (!is.numeric(min_value) | !is.numeric(max_value)) {
    stop("min_value and max_value must be numeric")
  }
  
  if (length(min_value) != 1 | length(max_value) != 1) {
    stop("min_value and max_value must be single values")
  }
  
  if (min_value >= max_value) {
    stop("min_value must be less than max_value")
  }
  
  case_when(
    measurements < min_value ~ NA_real_,
    measurements > max_value ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ measurements
  )
}

# Lab 10 Question 8-12 - Confidence interval coverage simulation
mycifun <- function(beta0, beta1, n) {
  x <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 1)
  ep <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  y <- beta0 + beta1 * x + ep
  
  data_sim <- tibble(x = x, y = y)
  model_lm <- lm(y ~ x, data = data_sim)
  
  out <- tidy(model_lm, conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(term == "x") |>
    transmute(
      slope_hat = estimate, 
      ci_low = conf.low, 
      ci_high = conf.high, 
      cover = if_else(beta1 >= ci_low & beta1 <= ci_high, 1L, 0L)
    )
  
  return(out)
}

# Run simulation 1000 times
set.seed(2024)
ci_dat <- map(.x = 1:1000,
              .f = ~mycifun(beta0 = 3, beta1 = 0.5, n = 100))
ci_results <- bind_rows(ci_dat)
simulated_coverage <- mean(ci_results$cover)

Revising My Thinking

Throughout the entire quarter, I have submitted revisions for assignments where I felt there was more for me to learn. This represents my commitment to learning from feedback, improving my work, and strengthening my R skills.

Early Quarter Revisions (Weeks 1-5)

Lab 3 Revisions - Key Learnings:

Revision 1: Data Description Context

Original Issue: My description only mentioned the structure (rows, columns, data types) without providing important context about where, when, how, and why the data were collected.

What I Learned: Understanding data context is essential for proper analysis and interpretation. I now automatically include who collected the data, when, for what purpose, and under what conditions in all my data descriptions. This deeper understanding helps me make better analytical decisions.

Revision 2: Code Formatting

Original Issue: My code line was too long (over 80 characters).

What I Changed: Added line breaks after pipes and commas to keep lines under 80 characters.

What I Learned: Code should have line breaks after pipes and commas for readability. I now automatically format my code properly in new assignments, making it more readable and professional. Good formatting isn't just aesthetic—it makes debugging easier and helps collaborators understand my work.

Revision 3: Function Syntax

Original Issue: I wasn't using explicit, named arguments in functions like if_any().

What I Changed: Updated to use .cols and .fns as named arguments with formula syntax ~ is.na(.x).

What I Learned: The if_any() function takes .cols and .fns as named arguments. Using formula syntax ~ is more explicit and follows tidyverse conventions. This reflection showed me why certain syntax matters, not just what is correct.

Challenge 3 Revisions - Key Learnings:

Revision 1: Visualization Labels

Original Issue: My plot was missing percentage labels that would make it easier to interpret.

What I Changed: Added geom_text() with position_fill() to display counts on the bars.

What I Learned: Using geom_text() with position_fill() adds labels. The after_stat() function accesses computed statistics. This taught me that visualizations should be self-explanatory without requiring readers to mentally calculate proportions.

Revision 2: Statistical Interpretation

Original Issue: My statistical conclusions lacked context about what the variables actually measured.

What I Changed: Rewrote conclusions to include what variables represent, not just statistical values.

What I Learned: Always provide context about what variables measure in conclusions. I now ensure my interpretations include what the variables actually mean rather than just citing statistical values.

Late Quarter Revisions (Weeks 7-10)

Lab 7 Revisions - Key Learnings:

Revision 1: Including All Requested Variables

Original Issue: I created a visualization that only included some of the requested variables (year and section) but not trip.

What I Changed: Modified the code to include all three requested variables (year, section, AND trip) and used paste() to create informative facet labels like "Trip 1" instead of just "1".

What I Learned: I need to carefully read requirements and include ALL requested components. When creating facets or groups, using descriptive labels (like "Trip 1") makes visualizations much more interpretable than just using raw values (like "1").

Revision 2: Side-by-Side Plot Display

Original Issue: Created two separate code chunks that output plots sequentially rather than side-by-side.

What I Changed: Used Quarto's layout-ncol: 2 chunk option to display plots side-by-side.

What I Learned: Quarto has special chunk options that control how figures are displayed. Using layout options allows direct visual comparison between related plots, which is essential for showing transformations or before/after comparisons.

Challenge 7 Revisions - Key Learnings:

Revision 1: Input Validation

Original Issue: My functions had no input validation to check if inputs were the correct type.

What I Changed: Added comprehensive checks for input types, lengths, and logical relationships.

What I Learned: Functions should validate inputs to ensure they're the correct type and make sense. Good input checks improve code reliability and provide helpful error messages. This is especially important when functions will be used by others or in production code.

Revision 2: Using case_when() Instead of Nested if_else()

Original Issue: Used nested if_else() statements which were harder to read.

What I Changed: Switched to case_when() for multiple conditions.

What I Learned: case_when() is built for multiple conditions and is more readable than complex if_else(). It also scales better when you need to add more conditions.

Revision 3: Legend Positioning

Original Issue: Legend at bottom made it harder to match lines to species in my time series plot.

What I Changed: Moved legend to the right and used fct_reorder2() to reorder legend items.

What I Learned: Legend on the right is easier to match with line positions than bottom placement. Using fct_reorder2() can reorder legend items to match the visual order of lines at the end of the plot, making interpretation much easier.
